analysis.one_liner: Repeals dozens of corporate tax breaks and requires companies to pay fair market value for public resources.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to six House committees in February 1997, drawn out across subcommittees, and died with zero cosponsors when the Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would end roughly two dozen special tax breaks used by oil and gas drillers, mining companies, timber growers, insurance companies, magazine publishers, and multinational corporations, and would require the government to stop selling public timber, minerals, grazing rights, water, and electricity for less than they are worth. It would charge mining companies an 8% royalty on minerals taken from federal land, set grazing fees at market rates, ban timber sales that lose the government money, and force national park concession contracts to be competitively bid. The revenue would reduce the deficit and fund cleanup of abandoned mines.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers generally, through deficit reduction and fairer returns on publicly owned resources, plus taxpayers who fund cleanup of abandoned mines and park improvements through new concession fees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers and users of public lands

how_it_helps.text: The bill bans selling any federal timber, minerals, forage, water, or hydroelectric power for less than fair market value, ending a long-standing practice of giving away public resources at a loss.

It would repeal special tax treatment for oil and gas (intangible drilling cost expensing, percentage depletion, the enhanced oil recovery credit, and the tertiary injectants deduction), hardrock mining, timber growing, and alcohol fuels.
Mining companies would pay a $100 annual fee per claim and an 8% royalty on production, with the money going to a fund to reclaim abandoned mines on federal lands.

Grazing fees on western public lands would be set at fair market value, below-cost timber sales from national forests would be prohibited, and oil and gas rentals on public lands would be set at market rates.
National park concession contracts would be competitively bid rather than automatically renewed, with franchise fees deposited for park maintenance and visitor services.
It would repeal tax exclusions for foreign sales corporations and deferral of income of controlled foreign corporations, ending benefits that let multinational companies shelter income abroad.

analysis.who_pays: Industries that currently receive the tax breaks and below-cost resource deals: oil and gas, hardrock mining, timber, ranching, insurance companies, publishers, and multinationals. Some costs would likely be passed to consumers and communities that depend on those industries. A few provisions would reach individuals directly, including taxing income of Americans living abroad and interest on state and local bonds.
analysis.who_pays_short: Energy, mining, timber, insurance, and agribusiness

drawbacks.text: The bill repeals the cash accounting method and the exclusion for cancelled farm debt that many farmers rely on, which would raise tax burdens on some family farms, not just large agribusiness.
It would tax the income of American citizens and residents living abroad, a change that would fall on individuals rather than corporations.
Repealing the federal tax exemption for state and local bond interest would raise borrowing costs for governments that finance schools, roads, and other public projects.
Repealing credits for electric vehicles, clean-fuel vehicles, and refueling property would remove incentives for cleaner transportation, a cost an environmental supporter would have to weigh.

The bill's breadth — six committees' worth of jurisdictions and dozens of separate repeals — made it easy for any affected industry or committee chair to find a reason to stop it, and it included no phase-ins or transition relief for most provisions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core idea — charging market prices for public resources and ending targeted corporate tax breaks — is straightforwardly pro-taxpayer, and much of it mirrors reforms later adopted piecemeal, such as mining claim fees. But the bill is indiscriminate: it sweeps in provisions whose costs fall on ordinary people, like taxing Americans' foreign income and municipal bond interest, and it would have raised costs for many small farms. A narrower bill would have been both fairer and more likely to pass.

outcome.mechanism: Referred to six House committees and scattered among ten subcommittees in February 1997; no committee ever acted on it, and it expired when the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Andrews introduced the Corporate Welfare Elimination Act of 1997 on February 4, 1997, with no cosponsors.
The bill was sent to six committees — Ways and Means, Commerce, Resources, Agriculture, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Budget — reflecting how many industries it touched.

Within three weeks it was further divided among subcommittees handling coast guard matters, energy and mineral resources, forests, national parks, water and power, and forestry; the last recorded action was on February 25, 1997.
No committee ever held a markup or reported the bill, no floor vote ever occurred, and it died at the end of the 105th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Industries that keep their tax breaks and below-cost public resource deals — oil and gas, hardrock mining, timber, grazing, insurance, and multinational corporations — along with their allies on the committees that never acted. Taxpayers forgo the revenue the bill would have raised.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Recipients of the tax breaks and cheap public resources

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Andrews
for.role: Sponsor, House Democrat from New Jersey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal corporate tax breaks and end below-cost sales of public resources.

against.name: Chairs of the six committees of referral
against.role: Ways and Means, Commerce, Resources, Agriculture, Transportation and Infrastructure, and Budget
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to subcommittees in February 1997 and never scheduled a markup or vote; the bill died in committee when the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and never reached a vote, so no partisan split can be measured — though its referral to committees chaired by Republicans meant the majority party controlled whether it ever moved.

industries.note: Would lose expensing of intangible drilling costs, percentage depletion, the enhanced oil recovery credit, and the tertiary injectants deduction, and would pay market-rate rentals on public lands. Its gain historically came at taxpayer expense through below-cost leases.

Would face a $100-per-claim annual fee, an 8% royalty on minerals taken from public land, a severance tax, and an end to patenting (buying) mining claims. Mining gold and other hardrock minerals from federal land for little or no royalty has been one of the clearest below-cost transfers of public wealth.
Below-cost timber sales from national forests — sales where the government loses money building roads and administering the sale — would be banned, and reforestation tax breaks repealed.

industries.industry: Livestock ranchers with federal grazing permits
industries.note: Grazing fees on western public lands would be set at fair market value, ending fees well below what private pasture costs.
The bill repeals the special tax treatment of Blue Cross and Blue Shield organizations, the small life insurance company deduction, and the alternative tax for small property and casualty insurers.
Repeal of the foreign sales corporation exclusion and of deferral of controlled foreign corporation income would raise taxes on companies shielding profits abroad.

Large farm operations would lose cash accounting, fertilizer and conservation deductions, and the farm debt cancellation exclusion, but the grazing, irrigation, and feed-assistance provisions hit mainly federal subsidy recipients. Some costs fall on ordinary family farms.

Concessioners would lose automatic preferential rights to renew contracts and face competitive bidding and franchise fees, but would gain protected possessory interests in improvements and contracts capped at ten to twenty years.

industries.industry: State and local governments and municipal bond investors
industries.note: Taxing municipal bond interest would raise state and local borrowing costs, affecting public projects and investors alike.
